content.text:
Nothing crashed on the device: the log shows no panics, stack canaries or reboots. Several of the ten run slowly, though, and I haven't seen what any of them look like. All the numbers below are from the serial log.

| Hack | fps | Step | Wait | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lightning | 29.4 | 1.8 ms | 0 | Fine. |
| Drift | 10.4 | 64 ms | 0 | Slowish, smooth enough. |
| Galaxy | 5.0–5.4 | 160–170 ms | 0 | Slow. |
| Discrete | 1.0–1.2 | 0.9–1.1 s | 0 | Far too slow. |
| Sphere | 30 | about 1 ms | 0 | Fine. |
| Spiral | 18.8 | 1 ms | 21 ms | Fine. The wait is the hack's own delay. |
| Thornbird | 29 | 2 ms | 0 | Fine, but see the heap point below. |
| FadePlot | 28 | 3 ms | 0 | Fine. |
| Sierpinski | 2.4 | 2 ms | 409 ms | Cheap to draw. The slow rate is its own 409 ms delay, so it's slow by design. |
| Vines | 2.8–3.0 | 133–160 ms | 175–187 ms | Slow by design plus a heavy step. |

- **Thornbird heap:** free internal heap fell from 317 KB to 648 bytes over about six seconds, then recovered fully when I switched to FadePlot. I read this as by design rather than a leak. The hack keeps 400 buffers of 100 rectangles, about 320 KB, filled one per frame. It's safe, but anything else that tried to allocate while Thornbird runs would fail.
- **Missing resources:** the `no default for resource 'cycles'/'count'` noise appeared as expected.
- **Not in the log:** Hopalong and Pyro's first lines are missing. The capture started on Pyro and your button presses went backwards from Lightning, so Hopalong never showed up.

**What I need from you**
1. What did each one look like? In particular, did Discrete and Galaxy still look right at 1 and 5 fps?
2. Which of the slow ones should stay: Discrete (1 fps), Galaxy (5), Drift (10), Vines and Sierpinski (about 3)? I won't drop anything on speed alone. My suggestion is to drop Discrete and keep the rest.
3. Should I record these numbers in `tools/assessment_measured.md`, regenerate the assessment, and then open the draft PR?

content.content:
## Measured on the device

Fourteen hacks have been run so far (default settings, 466×466 canvas pushed to
the display every frame, canvas held in PSRAM). The firmware times each frame
in three parts, averaged over 5 seconds: **step** is the hack's own draw call,
**push** is sending the canvas to the display, and **wait** is what is left of
the delay the hack asked for once the push is credited against it (the runner
caps any delay at 10 seconds). Rows other than Rorschach and Pedal were
measured before the cap was raised from 1 second; Helix also asks for 5-second
holds, so its frame rate will now be lower than shown.

| Hack | fps | step | push | wait | Extra PSRAM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pyro | 30.0 | 0.8-1.1 ms | 31.2 ms | 0 ms | about 80 KB |
| HyperCube | 28.3 | 2.7-2.9 ms | 31.5 ms | 0 ms | none measurable |
| Petri | 28.8-30.8 | 0.3-2.5 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 1.3 MB |
| XSpirograph | 11.0-11.4 | 54-56 ms | 31.4 ms | 0-20 ms | none measurable |
| Helix | 16.6-23.6 | 0.9-2.1 ms | 31.3 ms | 9-26 ms | none measurable |
| Rorschach | 3.0 | 0.6-1.7 ms | 31.1-31.2 ms | 367 ms | none measurable |
| Pedal | 0.2-0.4 | 126-519 ms | 31.4-31.5 ms | 3290-5507 ms | none measurable |
| Coral | 15.0-21.2 | 15-25 ms | 31.2 ms | 0-10 ms | about 240 KB |
| Squiral | 30.6-31.0 | 0.1-0.3 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 850 KB |
| Critical | 30.4 | 0.7 ms | 31.1 ms | 0 ms | about 15 KB |
| CloudLife | 24.2 | 8.8-8.9 ms | 31.4 ms | 0 ms | about 260 KB |
| WhirlWindWarp | 17.0-24.8 | 6.2-26.4 ms | 31.3 ms | 0 ms | about 410 KB |
| Flame | 1.8-7.4 | 76-592 ms | 31.4 ms | 0-72 ms | none measurable |
| Hopalong | 19.2-25.2 | 7.3-20.1 ms | 31.2-31.3 ms | 0 ms | about 8 KB |

Free heap and free PSRAM return to exactly the same values every time a
hack is switched back to, so switching does not leak.

## What limits the frame rate

- Pushing the 434 KB canvas costs a steady 31 ms whatever the hack draws, so
  about 31 fps is the real ceiling today. The best hacks reach about 30.
- A hack's delay is the pause after it draws, and the firmware credits only
  the 31 ms push against it. Hacks that ask for 10-20 ms therefore run at the
  push ceiling. Before the push was credited the delay was added on top, and
  Pyro, HyperCube and Petri ran at 22-23.5 fps. Crediting the whole step as
  well was tried and dropped: a hack asking for a hold got none once its own
  draw took that long, so slow Pedal pictures were erased as soon as they
  appeared.
- Rorschach and Pedal draw a picture and then hold it for the 5 seconds they
  ask for, so their frame rates (3.0 and 0.2-0.4) measure the holds, not the
  speed. Rorschach draws a picture in about 15 frames over half a second.
- XSpirograph is the slowest at drawing: 54-56 ms a frame for 1000 lines.
  Whether that is the PSRAM pixel writes or its double-precision maths has
  not been separated. Coral (15-25 ms), CloudLife (about 9 ms) and
  WhirlWindWarp (about 6 ms) are the next most expensive; Squiral and
  Critical draw in under a millisecond and run at the push ceiling.
- Coral's step time falls as the picture fills in (15.0 fps, then 21.2).
- Flame is the slowest hack so far. A frame takes about 76-80 ms for the
  cheap pictures and up to about 590 ms (1.8 fps) for the expensive ones,
  depending on the random flame it draws. Its source is all `double`, with
  `sin`, `cos` and `sqrt` in a recursive per-point loop, and the ESP32-S3 has
  only a single-precision FPU. Double-precision maths in software is the
  likely cause, but it has not been profiled. The scorer's `float-heavy` flag
  missed it, because it counts call sites in the source, not how often loops
  run it. A press made during such a step is kept and handled when the step
  ends (see Buttons below).
- WhirlWindWarp's step time sits on plateaus that change over time: about 6,
  8, 10, 19-20 and 25-26 ms across restarts, and it shifted within a single
  run (19.1, then 20.4, then 26.4 ms). It switches around 16 forcefields on
  and off at random, which fits, but which ones are expensive has not been
  identified.
- Free heap and PSRAM showed a single reading per hack across five restarts
  each of Flame and WhirlWindWarp, so repeated starts do not leak.
- Hacks that draw many primitives per frame are the ones to profile first.

## Other notes

Rorschach keeps a 9.6 KB array on the stack, which overflowed the Arduino
loop task's default 8 KB stack and rebooted the device on the first frame. The
firmware now sets a 16 KB loop stack (about 8 KB less free heap). Any hack with
large local arrays can hit the same limit.

Pyro's `init` builds two 6284-entry sine and cosine tables in double
precision, so restarting it dips to about 17 fps for a few seconds.

## Buttons

M5Unified reads the StopWatch buttons (GPIO2 for A and GPIO1 for B, active
low) only inside `M5.update()` and keeps no edge, so a press that began and
ended during one long hack step was never seen. The firmware now samples both
pins every 5 ms from a small task on core 0, and a latch counts a press once
the pin has held its new level for 30 ms. Repeated presses while a step runs
count as one, and holding a button does not repeat.

The serial switch line reports `press_waited`, the time from the press to the
switch. On the device it was usually 45-100 ms (the 30 ms settle plus one loop
period). Presses made during long steps waited for them: about 0.4 s on Flame
and 0.5-1.3 s around Pedal and Rorschach. About 90 switches, including bursts
of roughly four presses a second, showed no lost press, no reset and no
memory change.

A first version used GPIO interrupts and read the pin level when each ran.
The button bounced on release, the rising-edge interrupt saw the line low, and
the release was logged as a second press, so one click switched two hacks. The
polling design replaced it.

## Pedal

Pedal picks up to 1000 points per picture. The shim used to skip polygons
over 256 points, and the canvas dropped scanline crossings past 64, so half of
Pedal's pictures drew nothing. Both limits are gone. Sorting the crossings
with insertion sort then cost 2.6 million steps per picture on average and
21.6 million on the worst, which took about 4-5 seconds on the device; with
`qsort` above 16 crossings the step means are 126-519 ms. Pedal remains the
second most expensive hack to draw after Flame.

  64 ms) are the most expensive of the xlockmore batch; the rest run at or
  near the push ceiling. Vines and Sierpinski are slow because they ask for

  heap, filled one per frame, so free heap falls to under 1 KB after about
  six seconds. It is bounded, not a leak: switching away returned the heap
  to its earlier value.
"""
a="- Hacks that draw many primitives per frame are the ones to profile first.\n"
assert a in s
s=s.replace(a,note+a,1)
open(p,"w").write(s)

content.text:
I'm still on Galaxy and haven't changed any code yet. I need a decision from you first.

**Why it's slow:** each frame, every star (1500–3000 per galaxy, and `count: -5` gives 2–5 galaxies) is pulled towards every galaxy. That's double-precision `sqrt` maths in software, since the ESP32-S3 only has a single-precision FPU. I can't change that, because the hack has to stay byte-identical.

**What I can change:** the number of galaxies, which is the `count` resource. Setting it to 2 gives the classic pair of colliding galaxies instead of 2–5. By my estimate that is about 3× fewer star-galaxy interactions on average, so roughly 15–20 fps, close to Drift. I haven't measured it yet, so that's a guess.

**How I'd build it:** an on-device override list per hack. Our shim code would check it before the hack's own defaults, and the registry would carry `"*count: 2"` for Galaxy. I'd write the tests first, and Galaxy's source would stay untouched. The cost is a small new mechanism: one trailing field on `HackEntry`, one lookup layer in `resources.c`, and a line in `AGENTS.md`. Other slow hacks could use it later.

**Choices:**
1. Build the override and set Galaxy to `count 2`. I'd then host-test it, flash and measure. That needs your OK to re-flash.
2. Drop Galaxy: remove the registry entry, the notices row, the source file and the test-list entry.

I recommend option 1. It's cheap to try, and dropping stays available if the numbers disappoint. Which do you want?

file.content:
`xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in `hacks/registry.c` with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs the hack's
  `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`.
- Don't declare `xrealloc` or `xmalloc` in the shim: cloudlife defines its own
  static `xrealloc`, which would clash.
- `score_hacks.py` rates hacks by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps. Measure on the device.

content.text:
Galaxy now runs with two galaxies. The change is committed locally as `28958b1`, and it compiles and passes the host tests, but I haven't run it on the device.

- **How it works:** a `HackEntry` can now carry an `overrides` list that beats the hack's own defaults. Galaxy's list is `*count: 2`, so it gets a pair of colliding galaxies instead of 2–5. Galaxy's source is untouched. The registry has a new `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH` macro for this, and `AGENTS.md` documents it.
- **Tests:** I wrote them first and watched both fail. One is a resource-level test that an override wins over a hack's default and that clearing it restores the default. The other is a runner test that an entry's overrides apply to that hack only and don't leak into the next one. With the lookup order swapped, both failed. The full suite is 108/108 and `check_notices` is clean.
- **Device build and frame:** the device build succeeds. A dumped Galaxy frame at 200 frames shows a plausible swirling star field.
- **Speed guess:** by my estimate Galaxy should land around 15–20 fps. Please don't count on that until it's measured.

Can I flash and capture a short serial log (about 60 seconds, with Galaxy at index 22) so I can read its new step time? If it's still slow, my fallback is to drop it. Once you've seen it, the draft PR is next.

content.text:
Galaxy is now built in single precision, committed locally as `327b0a1`. It compiles and passes the host tests (108/108), but I haven't run it on the device.

**What was slow:** the `count` override did very little. Step time went from about 160 ms to 152 ms, and Galaxy's PSRAM use suggests it was already running two galaxies in both captures. The real cost is each star's `double` arithmetic, which the ESP32-S3 emulates in software at roughly 34 µs per star.

**What I changed:** the hack's source is untouched and still byte-identical (checked with `cmp`). A new file of ours, `hacks/galaxy_single.c`, includes the framework headers first, so shared structs keep their `double` layout. It then redefines `double` as `float` and `sqrt` as `sqrtf` before including `galaxy.c`, which each env's `build_src_filter` no longer compiles on its own. `AGENTS.md` documents this.

**Checks:** frames dumped from the float and double builds look the same at 200 and 600 frames. The float version is less precise, but nothing visible changed. The registry and notices check are fine, and the tools tests pass.

**Caveats:**
- **No test for the float build:** I didn't write a test that proves the float build is in use, because the only observable effect is speed. The device timing will be the check.
- **Speed guess:** I'd expect the step to fall from 152 ms to somewhere in the tens of milliseconds. I haven't measured it, so don't hold me to that. The `count 2` override stays in.

Can I flash this and capture another 90 seconds? If Galaxy is still slow, I'll drop it.

## Port ten xlockmore hacks

Ports the ten xlockmore hacks that compiled clean once the framework
landed: Vines, Sierpinski, FadePlot, Thornbird, Spiral, Sphere, Discrete,
Galaxy, Drift and Lightning. Each is byte-identical to xscreensaver 6.16
(checked with `cmp`), has a row in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, and is
registered after Hopalong in button order (indices 14-23).

### Changes beyond the hacks

- **`-DHAVE_MOBILE`** in all three PlatformIO envs. With two or more
  xlockmore hacks, each defined the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and the link failed. The flag turns that off;
  its only other effect on these hacks is an unread `*ignoreRotation: True`
  default.
- **Per-hack resource overrides.** `HackEntry` gains a trailing `overrides`
  list that is looked up before the hack's own defaults, registered with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`. Tests first, mutation-checked.
- **Galaxy in single precision.** `hacks/galaxy_single.c` (ours) includes the
  unmodified `galaxy.c` with `double` redefined as `float` and `sqrt` as
  `sqrtf`, because the ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only. `galaxy.c` is
  excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`. Host frames look the same.
  Galaxy also runs with `count: 2` through the new override.
- The xlock permission notice section in `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` is retitled
  so it covers all the xlockmore hacks.

### Measured on the device

| Hack | fps | Step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vines | 2.8-3.0 | 133-160 ms (plus 175-187 ms delay) |
| Sierpinski | 2.4-2.6 | 2-4 ms (plus 409 ms delay) |
| FadePlot | 28 | 3 ms |
| Thornbird | 29 | 2 ms |
| Spiral | 18.8 | 1 ms (plus 21 ms delay) |
| Sphere | 30 | 1 ms |
| Discrete | 1.0-1.2 | about 1 s |
| Galaxy | 13.4-14.2 | 38-42 ms (was 5 fps, 152 ms in double) |
| Drift | 10.4 | 64 ms |
| Lightning | 29.4 | 2 ms |

No panics, stack canaries or reboots. Rod looked at each on the device:
Discrete's slow updates fit the other deliberately slow hacks, Drift was
fine, and Galaxy is a lot better after the float build.

### Known notes

- Thornbird keeps about 320 KB of rectangle buffers in internal heap, so free
  heap drops to under 1 KB while it runs. It is bounded and recovers on
  switching away.
- Sphere, Drift, Lightning and Vines log `no default for resource 'count'` or
  `'cycles'` at start. The real framework treats those as 0, so it is noise.

### Testing

- Host: `pio test -e native` 108/108 under ASan; each hack runs 3000 frames
  and must draw within 2000.
- `pytest tools/tests` 64 passed; `tools/check_notices.py` clean.
- Device: flashed and measured as above.

content.text:
Probably yes, but I've only counted `double` and libm call sites in the source. I haven't profiled or measured any of these. Three look worth trying and the rest don't.

**Worth trying**

| Hack | Now on the device | Why it should benefit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete | about 1 s a frame | 21 `double` uses, 5 `sqrt`, 4 `sin`/`cos`. It's chaotic-map maths, and it's the slowest hack we have. |
| Flame | 1.8–7.4 fps (76–592 ms a step) | 16 `double` uses, plus `sin`, `cos`, `pow`, `exp` and `log`. It's the hack I'd already flagged as all-`double`. |
| Drift | 10 fps (64 ms) | 21 `double` uses and the same kind of iterated function system as Flame. |

For these three I'd redirect the libm calls as well (`sin` to `sinf`, `pow` to `powf` and so on), not just `sqrt`. Galaxy only needed `sqrt`, but these call the double-precision maths functions heavily.

**Probably not worth it**
- **Already single-precision or integer:** WhirlWindWarp uses `float`, and Coral and Sierpinski have no `double` at all.
- **Cheap already:** Hopalong (7–20 ms), Helix (1–2 ms), HyperCube (about 3 ms), Pyro and Lightning.
- **Slow for other reasons:** Pedal's time is polygon filling and sorting, and XSpirograph and Vines have only one or two `double` uses. In all three the cost is probably in our drawing shim. Vines also has a long built-in delay.

**Risks**
- **Precision:** these are chaotic maps, so float orbits will drift away from the double ones. The picture should look the same, since it's the overall shape that matters, but I'd check frames at several frame counts before flashing.
- **Where it would go:** these changes would add commits to the open PR #12, or go in a follow-up branch. I'd suggest a follow-up, so the PR you're reviewing doesn't change under you.

If you want, I'd start with Drift: it's the smallest change and has the clearest before-and-after. I'd generalise the wrapper first so every hack doesn't need its own copy. Then I'd try Discrete and Flame the same way. Each one would need your OK to flash and measure.

input.content:
## Single-precision builds for more hacks

Galaxy ran at 5 fps (152 ms a frame) because its per-star maths is `double`,
and the ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only, so `double` runs in
software. `hacks/galaxy_single.c` includes the unmodified `galaxy.c` with
`double` redefined as `float` and `sqrt` as `sqrtf`. That gave 14 fps
(38-42 ms) with frames that look the same on the host (PR #12).

The same trick may help other hacks. This is from counting `double` and libm
call sites in the source only; nothing here has been profiled.

### Candidates

| Hack | On the device now | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discrete | about 1 s a frame | 21 `double` uses, 5 `sqrt`, 4 `sin`/`cos` |
| Flame | 1.8-7.4 fps (76-592 ms a step) | 16 `double` uses, plus `sin`, `cos`, `pow`, `exp`, `log` |
| Drift | 10 fps (64 ms) | 21 `double` uses, an iterated function system like Flame |

### Not worth it

- Already `float` or integer: WhirlWindWarp, Coral, Sierpinski.
- Cheap already: Hopalong, Helix, HyperCube, Pyro, Lightning.
- Slow for other reasons: Pedal (polygon fill and sort), XSpirograph and
  Vines (one or two `double` uses, so the cost is probably in the shim).

### Approach

- Generalise the wrapper so each hack does not need its own copy, for
  example a small header or macro that redefines `double` and the libm calls.
- Redirect `sin`, `cos`, `pow`, `exp`, `log` and friends to their `f`
  variants too. Galaxy only needed `sqrt`; these hacks lean on the others.
- Include the framework headers before the redefinition so shared structs
  such as `ModeInfo` keep their `double` layout.
- Exclude the original `.c` from each env's `build_src_filter`, and keep it
  byte-identical (`cmp`).
- Start with Drift (smallest change, clearest before and after), then
  Discrete and Flame.

### Risks

- These are chaotic maps, so float orbits drift away from double ones. The
  overall picture should match, but dump frames at several frame counts and
  compare before flashing.
- Each one needs measuring on the device (fps, step time) before and after.

---
name: single-precision-build-for-double-heavy-hacks
description: Consider building double-heavy hacks as float via a wrapper (as done for Galaxy) when porting new ones
metadata:
  type: project
---

The ESP32-S3's FPU is single-precision only, so `double` maths runs in software and is slow. Galaxy went from 5 fps (152 ms a step) to 14 fps (38-42 ms) when built through `firmware/src/hacks/galaxy_single.c`: it includes the framework headers, then `#define double float` and `#define sqrt sqrtf`, then includes the unmodified `galaxy.c`, which is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.

**Why:** a per-hack `count` override did nothing for Galaxy; the cost was per-star `double` arithmetic. Hack source must stay byte-identical, so a compile-time wrapper is the only lever.

**How to apply:** when porting a hack, grep for `double`, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`, `pow`/`exp`/`log`. If it is double-heavy and slow on the device, try the wrapper (redirect the libm calls too, not just `sqrt`) and compare dumped frames at several frame counts before flashing. Candidates already identified: Discrete, Flame, Drift, filed as a GitHub issue (see [[stopwatch-device-gotchas]] for other device facts).

content.text:
The review found one thing, and it's a real bug that I introduced. I've fixed it and committed it locally as `eb936f8`, but I haven't pushed it.

**The finding** was high severity, at `registry.c:13`. With Galaxy's `count: 2` override, the hack skips its own cleanup when it restarts (`galaxy.c` only frees on `count < -2`). It still allocates fresh star rectangle buffers each time, so it leaked about 80 KB per restart. A restart happens roughly every 70 seconds at 14 fps, so leaving Galaxy running would eventually run out of memory. The 90-second serial capture was too short to show it.

**The fix:**
- **Test first:** `test_galaxy_restarts_do_not_leak_with_its_registered_overrides` runs the registered Galaxy entry with a short cycle so it restarts many times. It reads allocated bytes through ASan's `__sanitizer_get_current_allocated_bytes` and fails if they grow by 4 KB or more. It failed with the old override, which also served as the mutation check, and passes with the fix.
- **The change:** the override is now `count: -3`. That gives two or three galaxies and takes the cleanup path on restart.
- **Docs:** `AGENTS.md` and the measurements note now say `count: -3`.
- **Checks:** the full suite is 109/109, the device build succeeds and markdownlint passes.

**Speed is unmeasured:** the 14 fps figure came from a run with exactly two galaxies. With up to three, the step could rise to something like 60–90 ms on a bad draw. That's my estimate, not a measurement. The PR body and `assessment_measured.md` say so. Even at three galaxies it should beat the 5 fps we started with.

**Decisions for you:**
1. Push `eb936f8` to PR #12 and resolve the finding with a short note? Resolving needs the push first.
2. Flash and re-measure Galaxy with the new count? I'd do this before you merge.

content.text:
Galaxy runs at 9.4–11.2 fps on the device with `count: -3`. The fix is pushed to PR #12 and the finding is resolved. PR #12 is still a draft with the trail link intact.

| Galaxy | fps | Step | PSRAM used |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| At the start (152 ms) | 5 | 152 ms | about 294 KB |
| Single precision, 2 galaxies | 14 | 38–42 ms | about 200 KB |
| Single precision, `count: -3` | 9.4–11.2 | 58–75 ms | about 225–266 KB |

- **Capture:** it ran for 150 seconds, and the hack restarted once in that window with a different galaxy mix, which is why there are two timing bands. I saw no panics, stack canaries or reboots. A single restart can't prove there is no leak. The ASan test covers that, and it failed before the fix and passes now.
- **Speed:** it's slower than the two-galaxy run because the third galaxy adds work, but it's still about twice the original speed. If you'd rather have the faster version, `count: 2` is the only way to get exactly two galaxies, and it leaks on restart. A hybrid isn't possible without editing the hack.
- **Pushed:** `eb936f8` (the fix and test) and `82d3d9a` (the measurements) are on the branch. I also updated the PR body for the new numbers and the 109/109 test count.
- **Finding:** it's resolved with a note pointing at the fix, the test and the new measurement. `entire trail finding list 6` now shows none open.

The PR is ready for you to review and merge. Afterwards I'll delete the branch (remote and local) and fast-forward `main`.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/rod/.claude/skills/address-findings

# Address Findings

Fix and resolve the open review findings on an Entire trail. A finding is a
review comment posted to a trail on entire.io: it has a file/line location, a
body, a severity, and sometimes a suggested unified-diff patch. This skill
fetches the open findings, applies or hand-fixes each one in the current
worktree, and marks it resolved on the trail.

## When to use / not use

Use when the user points at a trail — a URL like
`https://<host>/<forge>/<owner>/<repo>/trails/<number>/<slug>`, or a bare trail
number or branch — and asks to **address / fix / resolve** its findings or
review comments.

Do **not** use this skill for:

- A code review of the current diff — that is the `review` skill (read-only).
- Creating new findings — use `entire trail finding add`.

## Response Format

Begin the first response to this skill invocation with the line:

`Entire Address Findings:`

followed by a blank line, then the content. Apply the header to the **first
response only**. Omit it on error / early-exit responses (CLI missing, not
authenticated, trail not found, branch mismatch, no open findings).

## Rules

1. Make the smallest correct change that addresses each finding. Do not expand scope.
2. Only mark a finding resolved when you actually addressed it. If a finding is
   ambiguous or needs a human decision, leave it open and report it.
3. Do not commit or push. Leave changes in the working tree for the user to review.
4. Never weaken a test or assertion just to clear a finding.

## Process

### 1. Verify the CLI

Run `entire version`. If the command is not found, stop and tell the user:
"The Entire CLI is required but not installed. Install it from
https://entire.io/docs/cli and try again."

### 2. Resolve the trail selector

- If the argument is a trail URL, take the number from the `/trails/<number>/`
  path segment and use that number.
- If it is a bare trail number, id, or branch name, use it as-is.
- If you cannot determine a trail, stop and ask the user for the trail URL or number.

Use this value as the `<trail>` selector for every command below. `entire trail`
accepts a trail number, id, or branch name interchangeably, so no number lookup
is needed — a branch name works directly.

### 3. Fetch open findings

```bash
entire trail finding list <trail> --json --status open
```

- If the output reports that authentication is required, stop and tell the user:
  "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- If the `trail finding` subcommand is unavailable, or the API reports the
  feature is not enabled, stop and tell the user that trail findings may not be
  enabled for this account or repository. Do not invent findings.
- Parse the JSON. Each finding has an id, a severity, a status, a body, a
  location (file path + line range), and may include a suggested change (a
  unified diff).
- If there are no open findings, report "No open findings on this trail." and stop.

### 4. Branch guard (you must be on the trail's branch)

`entire trail finding apply` edits the local worktree, so you must be on the
trail's branch before changing files.

```bash
git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD                # current branch
entire trail list --json --status any -n 200   # locate the trail's branch
```

Find the trail whose `number` or `branch` matches your selector and read its `branch`.

- If the trail's branch differs from the current branch, stop and tell the user:
  "Trail `<trail>` targets branch `<trail-branch>`, but you are on
  `<current-branch>`. Check it out first (`entire trail checkout <trail>`) and
  re-run." Do not edit files.
- If you cannot find the trail in the list (e.g. pagination), do not hard-fail:
  warn that you could not verify the branch, and ask the user to confirm they are
  on the trail's branch before you continue.

### 5. Address each finding

Process findings highest severity first (high → medium → low). For each:

1. **If it has a suggested unified-diff change**, dry-run it first:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --check
   ```

   If it applies cleanly, apply and resolve in one step:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding apply <trail> <finding-id> --resolve
   ```

2. **Otherwise** (no patch, the patch conflicts, or the fix needs reasoning):
   read the finding body, open the file at its location, and make the smallest
   correct edit that addresses it. If a fast, relevant local check exists for the
   touched code (a build or a focused test), run it. Then resolve:

   ```bash
   entire trail finding resolve <trail> <finding-id> -m "<one line: what you changed>"
   ```

3. **If you cannot confidently address it** (ambiguous, needs a product/design
   decision, or out of scope): leave it open, do not resolve it, and record it
   for the report.

### 6. Report

Summarize:

- Resolved via suggested patch — list finding ids and files.
- Resolved via manual edit — list finding ids, files, and a one-line of what changed.
- Left open for your decision — list finding ids and why.
- Any errors encountered.

Remind the user the changes are uncommitted and ready for review.

## Failure modes

- **CLI not installed** → install message (step 1).
- **Not authenticated** → "`entire trail finding list` requires authentication. Run `entire login` and try again."
- **Trail findings not enabled / API error** → tell the user the feature may be
  unavailable; do not fabricate findings.
- **Trail not found** → tell the user to check the URL or number; suggest
  `entire trail list --status any`.
- **Wrong branch** → stop with the checkout instruction (step 4).
- **Patch does not apply** → fall back to a manual edit; if you cannot fix it
  confidently, leave the finding open and report it.
- **Not a git repository** → stop and tell the user to run from inside the trail's repo.

content.text:
All four open findings are on hacks that have to stay byte-identical to xscreensaver 6.16, and I judge none of them to be a bug on this device. I changed nothing and left all four open.

| Finding | Severity | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `fadeplot.c:196`: int overflow in the `stab[...]` index | high | Not a bug here (see below). |
| `galaxy.c`: `double` coordinate cast to `short` can overflow | medium | Upstream behaviour in the hack's own code. |
| `thornbird.c:217`: same cast, from chaotic values | low | Upstream behaviour. |
| `discrete.c`: same cast, for variations that can grow unbounded | low | Upstream behaviour. |

- **FadePlot (high):** the index is `st.x + speed.x*j + i*step.x`, which can't overflow or go negative at these sizes.
  - `st.x` is below `angles`, which is under 1,200.
  - `speed.x` is at most 30.
  - `j` is below `nbstep`, and `i` is below `maxpts/nbstep`, at most 150 with the default 1500 cycles.
  - `step.x` is 1, because the ×3 scaling only applies above a 2,560-pixel canvas.
  - The largest index is a few thousand, and the `% angles` keeps it in range anyway.
- **Galaxy, Thornbird and Discrete (cast overflow):** an out-of-range `double`-to-`short` cast does happen in these hacks, and it's the same in upstream xscreensaver. On the ESP32 it produces a wrapped coordinate, which draws a stray point somewhere else. It can't crash, because the shim clips every rectangle and point it draws. Fixing it would mean editing the hack, which the byte-identical rule forbids. A shim-side fix isn't possible either, since the cast happens before the shim sees the value.

I haven't committed or pushed anything, and there's nothing in the working tree beyond Entire's own `.entire/settings.json`.

I can dismiss these on the trail with a note giving the reasons above, but I've left them open since you didn't ask for that. Shall I?

### Update: `AGENTS.md`, "Adding a hack"

**Why:** the Galaxy work showed that double-heavy hacks are slow on this chip, and a hack-specific override can break the hack's own cleanup.

```diff
+7. If a hack is slow and `double`-heavy (many `double`s, `sqrt`, `sin`/`cos`,
+   `pow`), try a single-precision wrapper like `hacks/galaxy_single.c`
+   (candidates in issue #13). A resource override can skip a hack's restart
+   cleanup: Galaxy leaked at `count: 2`, so leak-test any override.
```

### Update: `AGENTS.md`, "Commands" (serial log bullet)

**Why:** a flash piped through `head` may have been killed by SIGPIPE, and the button direction surprised both of us.

```diff
+- Flash with `pio run -e stopwatch -t upload > file 2>&1`, never piped through
+  `head`, and check for "Hash of data verified". The button steps backwards
+  (Pyro, then Lightning, then Drift...), and a hack that restarts every ~70 s
```

## Delivering a branch

- `entire trail create --title ... --type feature --body ...` pushes the branch
  and opens a linked DRAFT PR. The PR body is not synced from the trail: update
  both (`entire trail update --body`, `gh pr edit N --body-file`). Put
  `Fixes #N` in the body.
- Rod approves and merges (merge commit). Afterwards delete the merged branch
  (remote and local) without asking and fast-forward `main`.
- Findings: `entire trail finding list N`, then `... resolve N <id> -m "..."`.
  Bot reviews can lag about 20 minutes.

## Gotchas
- `score_hacks.py` rates hacks by call sites, not loop trips: Flame (all
  `double` maths) is rated S but runs at 2-7 fps. Measure on the device.
- `pio test` runs every registered hack for 3000 frames under ASan (about 15 s);
  a hack that is slow on the host slows the whole suite.
- zsh does not word-split `$var`: loop over file lists with `bash -c`.

which every PlatformIO env and `score_hacks.py` set; without it they
  include `xlock.h` instead. The envs also define `HAVE_MOBILE`, because
  otherwise each hack's `XSCREENSAVER_LINK` defines the same global
  `xscreensaver_function_table` and two hacks fail to link; the only other
  effect is an inert `*ignoreRotation: True` default. Register one in `hacks/registry.c` with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK(<name>, "<Class>")`. The runner runs the hack's
  `setup_cb` once and passes `setup_arg` as `init_cb`'s hidden third
  argument, as xscreensaver's `screenhack.c` does. Its table is empty until
  then. Resources the framework reads but a hack does not define
  (`delta3d`, `size`, ...) fall back to `kFrameworkDefaults` in
  `x11shim/resources.c`. A `HackEntry`'s `overrides` list beats the hack's own
  defaults (Galaxy runs with `count: -3`, at most three galaxies; a count of -2 or
  above skips the hack's restart cleanup and leaks); register it with
  `XLOCKMORE_HACK_WITH`.
  Galaxy is built through `hacks/galaxy_single.c`, which includes the unmodified
  `galaxy.c` with `double` redefined as `float` (the S3's FPU is single-precision
  only); `galaxy.c` is excluded from each env's `build_src_filter`.

content.text:
This is a bounded change: it extends `galaxy_single.c`, which already exists, so I'll give you a short design and wait for your yes before touching anything. `main` is clean.

**What I found:** Drift and Discrete are xlockmore hacks, and Flame is a plain screenhack. All three use libm well beyond `sqrt`: `sin`, `cos`, `atan`, `atan2`, `exp`, `fabs` and, in Discrete, `fmod`. So the wrapper has to redirect those calls too, not just `sqrt` as Galaxy's does.

**Design**
1. **Shared header:** `hacks/single_precision.h` (ours) defines `double` as `float` and redirects the libm calls to their `f` versions (`sinf`, `cosf`, `atanf`, `atan2f`, `expf`, `fabsf`, `fmodf`, `sqrtf`, `powf` and `logf`). It ends with `_Static_assert(sizeof(double) == 4, ...)`. That is a compile-time test: if the redefinition is dropped, the build fails.
2. **Wrappers:** each gets a small `hacks/<name>_single.c` that includes the system and framework headers first (so shared structs keep their `double` layout), then the shared header, then the unmodified `<name>/<name>.c`.
3. **Galaxy moves onto the shared header too.** The only change for it is that its init-time `sin` and `cos` become the `f` versions. I'll check its frames are unchanged.
4. **Build:** each original `.c` is excluded in the three `build_src_filter` lines, as with Galaxy. The registry doesn't change.
5. **Order:** Drift first (smallest change), then Discrete, then Flame. Each is its own commit and gets a host double-versus-float frame comparison at several frame counts before anything is flashed.
6. **Device:** I'll ask before each flash. We have baselines from before: Drift 64 ms, Discrete about 1 s, Flame 76–592 ms a step.
7. **Delivery:** a branch `feature/single-precision-hacks` with a draft PR containing `Fixes #13`, once measured and with your go-ahead.

**Risks**
- **Visual drift:** these are chaotic systems, so float orbits will diverge from the double ones. If a hack visibly looks worse, I'll leave it in double and record why.
- **Flame:** it installs a `SIGFPE` handler. That shouldn't matter on the ESP32, but I'll watch for it.
- **Test coverage:** the compile-time assert covers "is float in use". The existing host tests cover "still draws". Whether it's faster is only visible on the device.

Shall I go ahead on that basis?
